clue.text: Bacterium in rum real, is it?

blocks.note: the eight anagram letters, posing as the setter's own doubt

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' means odd or strange — a classic anagram signal — and the mock-hesitant 'is it?' is not doubt but fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Listeria is the food-poisoning bacterium named after the pioneering surgeon Joseph Lister.

clue.text: Setter in a dress that’s short

blocks.note: the article supplies its own letter
a dress is GARB; 'that's short' cuts off the final letter

explanation.walkthrough: The surface dangles a crossword setter in a frock; the real setter works in the kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: Agar is the seaweed-derived gelling agent that makes jellies set — a 'setter' in the culinary sense.

clue.text: Belly squeezed by fifth columnist in squat

blocks.note: your tum is your belly
a fifth columnist is an enemy agent working within — a spy

explanation.walkthrough: A fifth columnist really is a spy, so the wordplay hides inside a plain description rather than an instruction. 'Squat' is wanted as an adjective, not as the crouch.
explanation.definitionFit: Squat and stumpy both describe a short, thick-set build — everyday synonyms, both adjectives.

clue.text: Nobody drunk now nobody drinks!

blocks.note: the answer runs straight across all three words: drUNK NOW Nobody

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drinks' pictures the phrase swallowing the answer whole — a hidden word stretched across three words of a strangely teetotal scene.
explanation.definitionFit: An unknown is a person the public has never heard of — just what we mean by a nobody.

clue.text: Activation of lever in bed to get warmer at night?

blocks.note: 'activation of' sets the lever's letters moving
a cot is a bed — it wraps around the shuffled lever

explanation.walkthrough: An anagram tucked inside a container: the activated LEVER climbs into the COT. The question mark excuses the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A coverlet is a bedspread — the top layer that keeps a sleeper warm through the night.

clue.text: Inferior boss, decent after training

blocks.note: the ten anagram letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'After training' does the rearranging — the boss emerges decent, but still only second-best.
explanation.definitionFit: Something second-best is by definition not quite the best, and so inferior to it — an adjective, as in 'a second-best effort'.

clue.text: Knight guzzling absinthe, originally on the wagon

blocks.note: 'originally' takes just the two initial letters
a wain is an old word for a farm wagon

explanation.walkthrough: 'On the wagon' means teetotal, which is exactly what the absinthe is there to contradict. In a down clue 'on' simply stacks one piece above another.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Gawain was one of King Arthur's knights of the Round Table, hero of 'Sir Gawain and the Green Knight'.

clue.text: More than one man mountain somewhere in 15

blocks.note: chess and draughts call their pieces men, and kings are the grandest of them
informally, a mountain of work is a ton of it

explanation.walkthrough: Paul splits the phrase 'man mountain' in two and clues each half separately — the misdirection is in the join.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingston is Jamaica's capital city, so it sits on the island that 15 across names.

clue.text: Love and prayer in 15 breaks through for Willard White, perhaps

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis
a Rastafarian — Jamaica's man of prayer
as in 'per head' = 'for each' — even this little word is wordplay

explanation.walkthrough: The step that unlocks it is reading 'prayer' as a person rather than something said. 'For' looks like joinery and is building material — Paul rarely wastes a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Willard White is the Jamaican-born operatic bass — 'perhaps' flags him as one example of an opera star.

clue.text: See 9
Python catches boa wandering by say, somewhere in 15

blocks.note: Monty Python — the comedy troupe, not the snake
the snake that really is here, sent 'wandering'
'say' = for example = e.g.

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the Python is a comedy troupe and the boa is only letters — two snakes in one clue and neither of them real. 'Say' for e.g. is a workhorse worth banking.
explanation.definitionFit: Montego Bay is Jamaica's famous resort city on the north coast — another somewhere on the island of 15.

clue.text: Hard left turns approaching end of rally – something for the winner?

blocks.note: H = hard, as on pencils
the nautical left
'end of' takes the last letter of 'rally'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Turns' spins the whole of H + PORT round in one go before it meets the tail of 'rally'.
explanation.definitionFit: A trophy is the silverware handed to whoever wins — the question mark winks at the rally-driving surface.

clue.text: Thing concluding film featuring final lightweight item

blocks.note: slang: your bag is your thing, as in 'not my bag'
a pic is a picture — a film
this is what PIC 'features' — LAST goes inside

explanation.walkthrough: 'Thing' for a bag comes straight out of 'not my bag', and it is the best moment in the clue. 'Concluding' is positional rather than definitional: it says where a piece goes, not what it means.
explanation.definitionFit: A plastic bag weighs next to nothing — a literally lightweight item, whatever the surface's talk of closing credits.

clue.text: Hats off, supply a wrap

blocks.note: a well is a source or supply, as in 'a well of sympathy'
film-set slang: 'that's a wrap' means it's finished — done

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'supply' as a noun and 'a wrap' as the end of filming, and the congratulation assembles itself.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Well done!' and 'hats off!' are both exclamations congratulating someone on a job admirably completed.

clue.text: Was she not given a choice to speak for country?

blocks.clueFragment: Was she not given a choice
blocks.note: 'ja make 'er?' asks whether she was forced to go

explanation.walkthrough: The old music-hall gag: 'My wife's gone to the West Indies.' 'Jamaica?' 'No, she went of her own accord.'
explanation.definitionFit: Jamaica is the Caribbean island country the whole puzzle keeps returning to — the plain geographical definition.

clue.text: Rodent taking wodge around lunchtime?

blocks.note: a wodge is a thick lump — a chunk
1pm, with a Roman numeral I standing for the 1

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lunchtime?' is 1pm — written with a Roman I — a lovely bit of setter's sleight of hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A chipmunk is the small striped North American ground squirrel — a rodent, plainly defined.

clue.text: Oath’s not a pretence, would Aussie say?

blocks.note: what is no pretence is the truth — ''s truth', short for 'God's truth'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Strewth' contracts 'God's truth', and the truth is exactly what a pretence is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Strewth is a mild exclamation of surprise — an oath in the swearing sense, stereotypically heard from Australians.

clue.text: Frivolous throw, cast and pitch?

blocks.note: count them: three synonyms, and TRI is the prefix for three
then read the same list for what it means: all three of them are a FLING

explanation.walkthrough: Count the synonyms: throw, cast and pitch are three flings, and the question mark admits the cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: Trifling means trivial, of no consequence — 'a trifling sum' is a frivolous one; both words are adjectives.

clue.text: Periods on horseback where British king into himself?

blocks.note: the United Kingdom
K = king, as in chess notation
Chas, short for Charles — the British king himself

explanation.walkthrough: Reading 'himself' as the king's own familiar name is the step that unlocks it. The clue also reads straight through as a description of polo, which is the fun of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A chukka is one of the timed periods a polo match is divided into — and polo is played on horseback.

clue.text: See 26
Counter when a god denied church

blocks.note: A, then Bacchus, the Roman god of wine
the abbreviation that 'denied' strips out of Bacchus

explanation.walkthrough: Bacchus loses his CH — denied church — and what remains counts beads, not blessings.
explanation.definitionFit: An abacus is the bead-frame used for counting — a counter in the calculating sense, not a shop's.

clue.text: Old man’s taken to island, 15 by the sound of it?

blocks.note: your old man is your pa
supplies its own letters
the standard map abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: PA is packed off: 'to' gives itself and 'island' shrinks to IS — a gentle build under a lovely definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Patois is Jamaican creole — what 15 across sounds like when it speaks, hence '15 by the sound of it'.

clue.text: Ralph snatches ‘er wig

blocks.note: to ralph is slang for to vomit — to puke
'her' with the aitch dropped

explanation.walkthrough: Not a man's name at all: 'ralph' is slang for being sick, and PUKE grabs the dropped-aitch 'er.
explanation.definitionFit: A peruke is the long powdered wig worn in the 17th and 18th centuries — a period word for a hairpiece.

clue.text: One struck by god, Cupid

blocks.note: a match is something you strike
the Maker — God as creator

explanation.walkthrough: 'One struck by god' sounds like a thunderbolt victim; really it is a struck match beside the Maker.
explanation.definitionFit: Cupid, whose arrows pair lovers off, is the archetypal matchmaker — a definition by example from myth.

clue.text: See 25
Bellyache – something in 15’s patty?

blocks.note: to bellyache is to complain or gripe about something
the type of red meat that's the classic filling for a Jamaican patty

explanation.walkthrough: Two meanings split by the dash: the grumble, and the filling of Jamaica's best-loved pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: To beef is to gripe or bellyache, while beef is also the spiced meat that fills a Jamaican patty.

clue.text: Favourite from 15 in sprint past team featuring Gatlin, Gay etc?

blocks.note: Justin Gatlin and Tyson Gay sprinted for the United States
used just as it stands
to sprint is to bolt

explanation.walkthrough: Gatlin and Gay were Bolt's great American rivals — here reduced to the team he sprints past.
explanation.definitionFit: Usain Bolt, the fastest sprinter in history, is Jamaica's national hero — the island's favourite son.

clue.text: A fantastic island chef takes dish from 15

blocks.note: the first of the sixteen anagram letters
the rest of the fodder for 'fantastic' to cook up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fantastic' cooks all sixteen letters at once — a whole island chef goes into the pot for Jamaica's national dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Ackee and saltfish — buttery ackee fruit scrambled with salted cod — is Jamaica's beloved national dish.
